stimulus:
An Arab chronicler writing around 1220 described the Mongol invaders of the Islamic world — whom he called Tatars — as warriors who spared no one, killing men, women, and children alike. He observed that they traveled with great herds of sheep, cattle, and horses, carrying their food supply with them, so that when they arrived anywhere they 'had need of nothing from without.' He also noted their unfamiliar customs, including worship of the sun at its rising and dietary practices that shocked his readers.

The observation illuminates the campaigns of 1219–1223 that shattered the Khwarazmian Empire. Cities that surrendered were generally spared and taxed; cities that resisted — Samarkand, Bukhara, Merv — were stormed and their populations massacred as a warning to the next city. The chronicler wrote in the midst of these events, recording reports of whole regions emptied by an army that needed nothing from the lands it crossed.
stem: The chronicler's observation about the invaders' herds most directly helps explain which of the following?
options: (A) Why the invaders quickly adopted the settled farming practices of the lands they conquered
(B) Why the invaders avoided pitched battles and preferred to fight only at sea
(C) Why the invaders depended on tribute payments from merchant cities to feed their animals
(D) Why the invaders could campaign far from settled lands and move faster than most sedentary armies
explanation: Steppe pastoralists like the Mongols carried their food with them in the form of livestock, so they did not need slow supply trains or friendly farmland. This gave their armies extraordinary speed and range, letting them strike deep into distant territories. That is exactly what the chronicler noticed: an army that 'had need of nothing from without.'

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Mongols remained pastoralists; they did not settle down to farm the lands they conquered.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Mongols were a land power famous for open-field cavalry battles, not naval warfare.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The whole point of the chronicler's observation is that the herds made tribute unnecessary for feeding the army.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Mobile herds freed Mongol armies from supply lines, which explains their rapid, long-distance campaigns.

stimulus:
An Arab chronicler writing around 1220 described the Mongol invasion of the Islamic world as a calamity unlike any other: the invaders, he wrote, spared neither women nor children, and their deeds 'horrify all who hear of them.' He presented the invasion as a catastrophe visited upon Islam and its peoples, and could barely bring himself to record what had happened.

The devastation he describes fell hardest on the cities of Persia and Central Asia — Merv, Nishapur, Herat — whose artisans were killed or enslaved and whose irrigation works were wrecked. Yet within a generation, Mongol rulers were rebuilding many of these same cities as administrative centers: sponsoring observatories and workshops, repairing canals, and guaranteeing the safety of merchants on the overland routes. The chronicler, writing at the moment of destruction, could not see the reconstruction that followed.
stem: A historian studying the revival of long-distance Eurasian trade in the later 1200s would most reasonably treat this passage as
options: (A) evidence that contemporary observers welcomed the Mongols as restorers of order
(B) the best available record of the volume of goods traded along the Silk Road
(C) direct proof that Mongol conquests made all Eurasian trade impossible for the rest of the century
(D) vivid evidence of the violence of the initial conquests, but a limited guide to how Mongol rulers later treated merchants
explanation: The passage captures the trauma of the conquest years, when cities that resisted were destroyed. But it was written at the moment of invasion, before Mongol rulers established the policies of the later 1200s — protecting merchants, guaranteeing safe passage, and encouraging trade across Eurasia. A source shaped by the shock of conquest cannot show us the administrative choices that came afterward.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The author's horror is the opposite of a welcome; he calls the invasion an unprecedented calamity.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The passage contains no figures or commercial detail about trade volumes.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Trade across Eurasia actually revived under later Mongol rule; the passage describes the conquest, not the decades that followed.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The passage documents conquest-era violence well, but its author's perspective cannot reveal later Mongol commercial policies.

stimulus:
When Mongol armies conquered a city, they routinely spared certain captives: skilled weavers, metalworkers, engineers, astronomers, and physicians. These specialists were often relocated hundreds or thousands of miles — Chinese siege engineers to Persia, Persian astronomers to China — to serve the Mongol court and its armies.

The practice was systematic, not incidental. Mongol rulers surveyed each conquered city for talent: Samarkand yielded weavers, Beijing yielded engineers. The relocated specialists served the court directly — building siege engines for the next campaign, weaving cloth-of-gold for the khans, casting astronomical instruments. In this way, a technique mastered at one end of Eurasia could be put to work at the other within a single generation.
stem: The practice described in the passage is best understood as serving which of the following Mongol aims?
options: (A) Gathering skilled workers to strengthen the empire's administration, crafts, and weaponry
(B) Converting conquered peoples to the Mongols' own religious beliefs
(C) Resettling the Mongolian steppe with settled farmers from conquered lands
(D) Punishing defeated cities by permanently removing their most prominent families
explanation: The Mongols were pragmatists. Rather than destroying useful talent, they collected it: engineers built their siege weapons, astronomers staffed their observatories, and artisans produced goods for the court. Moving specialists across the empire also spread techniques between regions, which is one reason the Mongol period saw so much cross-cultural exchange.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The selective sparing and relocation of specialists was a deliberate policy to harness conquered peoples' skills.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Mongols were famously tolerant in religious matters and made no systematic effort to convert their subjects.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Mongols had no interest in farming the steppe; they preserved it as pasture for their herds.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Deportation was about acquiring talent, not punishment — the specialists were put to work, not discarded.

stimulus:
The Mongol invasions of the 1200s shattered the political order of the Islamic heartland. Baghdad, the seat of the Abbasid caliphate for five centuries, was sacked in 1258. Yet within a few decades, the Mongol rulers of Persia — the Ilkhans — began converting to Islam, and by the early 1300s the Ilkhan Ghazan was sponsoring mosques, patronizing Persian scholars, and presenting himself as a Muslim sovereign.

The change was personified at the top: the dynasty founded by Hülegü, the conqueror who ordered Baghdad's destruction, produced rulers who built mosques, endowed religious schools, and corresponded with the Mamluk sultans of Egypt as fellow Muslim sovereigns. Persian bureaucrats — the same class that had served the caliphs — staffed the Ilkhanid administration, keeping the tax registers in Persian and running the empire's daily business. Conquest gave way to accommodation, and the conquerors adopted the civilization of the conquered.
stem: Which of the following best describes the longer-term outcome of the conquests for the lands of the former Abbasid realm?
options: (A) The Islamic world was reunified under a single restored caliphate
(B) Persian ceased to be used as a language of administration in favor of Mongolian
(C) The Mongol rulers of Persia converted to Islam and became patrons of Islamic institutions
(D) Islamic political and cultural life came to a permanent end in the Middle East
explanation: The conquests destroyed the Abbasid caliphate, but they did not destroy Islam in the region. The Ilkhanid Mongols, ruling a Muslim-majority population, converted — most decisively under Ghazan in 1295 — and governed as Muslim monarchs within a Persianate administrative tradition. Islamic scholarship, law, and architecture continued under their patronage.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. No single caliphate was restored; the region remained divided among competing states.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Persian remained the language of administration and high culture under the Ilkhans.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Ilkhans' conversion shows how conquerors were absorbed by the culture of the conquered.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Islam remained the dominant religion and a thriving cultural force in the region long after the conquests.

stimulus: A linguistic map of Africa shows the Niger-Congo language family divided into branches. One branch, the Bantu languages, is shaded dark gray and covers most of the continent south of the equator — from the Atlantic coast to the Indian Ocean — while other branches cluster mainly in West Africa.
stem: The spread shown on the map was most directly made possible by which of the following?
options: (A) Ironworking and farming knowledge, supporting population growth and settlement
(B) The use of horse cavalry to conquer neighboring peoples rapidly
(C) The adoption of a common written script that unified diverse communities
(D) The establishment of large coastal trading empires before 1000 CE
explanation: The Bantu expansion was a slow migration of farming peoples, not a military conquest. Iron tools let them clear forests for fields, and productive agriculture supported population growth that pushed settlement steadily outward over many centuries. That agricultural package is what carried their languages across half a continent.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Iron tools and farming were the material foundation of the Bantu migrations.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Horses could not thrive in much of sub-Saharan Africa because of the tsetse fly, and the Bantu spread was not a cavalry conquest.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Bantu societies transmitted knowledge orally; shared writing arrived much later with Arabic and Latin scripts.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The great coastal trading states, such as the Swahili cities, developed later and were a separate phenomenon.

stimulus: A linguistic map of Africa shows the Niger-Congo language family divided into branches. One branch, the Bantu languages, is shaded dark gray and covers most of the continent south of the equator — from the Atlantic coast to the Indian Ocean — while other branches cluster mainly in West Africa.
stem: Which statement about the map reflects the best historical thinking?
options: (A) The map shows that the Bantu expansion was caused by the spread of Islam
(B) The map demonstrates that no other language families existed anywhere in Africa
(C) The shading compresses centuries of migration into a single snapshot
(D) The map proves that all Bantu languages were identical everywhere they were spoken
explanation: A map is a snapshot, but the Bantu expansion took more than two thousand years. The dark shading compresses countless small migrations into one image. Reading it correctly means remembering that the languages spread gradually, diverged as they went, and looked different at every point along the way.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Bantu expansion began long before Islam reached sub-Saharan Africa.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Africa has several other major language families, including Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Good map reading means restoring the dimension of time that the image flattens.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Bantu languages diverged greatly over time and distance; shared shading does not mean identical speech.

stimulus: A linguistic map of Africa shows the Bantu branch of the Niger-Congo family covering most of sub-Saharan Africa. Along the Indian Ocean coast, port towns such as Kilwa and Mombasa grew wealthy from maritime trade, and in these towns a new language took shape: Swahili, built on Bantu grammar with a large Arabic vocabulary.
stem: The development of Swahili along the East African coast best illustrates which of the following processes?
options: (A) The spread of Islam by missionaries with no connection to commerce
(B) The migration of Bantu speakers back toward the Arabian peninsula
(C) Bantu speech blending with Arabic through Indian Ocean trade
(D) The imposition of Arabic on East Africa by conquering Arab armies
explanation: Swahili was born in the trading towns where African, Arab, and Persian merchants met. Its grammar is Bantu, but centuries of commercial and cultural contact layered thousands of Arabic words into it. The language is a record of exchange, not conquest.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Islam spread along the coast largely through the same merchant networks that carried goods.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The movement went the other way — Bantu languages spread south and east within Africa.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Swahili's mixed character directly reflects the commercial blending of the Swahili coast.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. No Arab army conquered East Africa; Arabic arrived with traders, not invaders.

stimulus:
In early-1400s France, Christine de Pizan — widowed young and left to support her family — became one of Europe's first women to earn a living as a professional writer. In her 'Book of the City of Ladies,' she stages a dialogue with a personified figure of Reason, asking why women are excluded from courts of law and answering the learned men who claimed women were naturally inferior.

Widowed at twenty-five with three children and a mother to support, de Pizan chose not to remarry — an unusual decision — and turned to the one marketable skill she possessed: an exceptional education, rare for a woman of her time. Her father, astrologer to King Charles V, had seen to her learning. Her patrons came to include Queen Isabeau of Bavaria and the dukes of Burgundy and Orléans, and over three decades she produced histories, political counsel, and defenses of women — the first woman in Europe known to have lived entirely by her pen.
stem: De Pizan's career as a professional writer was most directly made possible by which feature of late-medieval European society?
options: (A) The Protestant emphasis on individual Bible reading
(B) Literate court culture and aristocratic patronage in growing cities
(C) The spread of printing presses that let authors reach mass audiences
(D) The admission of women to universities
explanation: De Pizan wrote for paying patrons at the French royal court and among the nobility — a literate, wealthy audience concentrated in cities. That patronage system is what allowed a widow with no institutional position to support herself by writing.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Reformation began a century after her death.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Court patronage created a market for writers outside the church and universities.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. De Pizan died around 1430, before Gutenberg's press; her books circulated as hand-copied manuscripts.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Medieval universities did not admit women as students or teachers.

stimulus:
In her 'Book of the City of Ladies' (1405), Christine de Pizan stages a dialogue with three allegorical figures — Reason, Rectitude, and Justice — who help her build an imaginary city populated by accomplished women of history. Through conversation with these personifications, she refutes the claims of male authors who wrote that women were naturally inferior to men.

The allegorical debate was a familiar medieval device: writers staged arguments between personified abstractions — Nature and Reason, Body and Soul — to explore contested questions. De Pizan knew the tradition intimately. But she bent it to a new purpose: where earlier authors had used such dialogues to rehearse the learned case against women, drawn from Aristotle and the Church Fathers, she had Lady Reason systematically demolish that case, answering slander with the documented achievements of real and legendary women. In de Pizan's hands, the old form carried a new argument: that the authorities cited against women proved nothing, because the men who wrote them had never truly known their subject.
stem: The passage's form — a dialogue with personified figures like Reason — most directly reflects the influence of which of the following?
options: (A) The classical Greek theater revived by Renaissance humanists
(B) The Islamic hadith collections recording sayings of the Prophet
(C) The Protestant catechism's question-and-answer format
(D) The medieval tradition of allegorical debate and scholastic dialogue
explanation: De Pizan was working inside a familiar medieval literary form: the debate conducted through allegorical personifications, related to the scholastic habit of arguing through dialogue. Her innovation was to turn that traditional form against misogynist writing.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The passage is prose dialogue, not drama, and it predates the humanist revival of Greek theater.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Hadith collections record reported sayings; they do not stage debates with personified abstractions.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The catechism format belongs to the Reformation, a century after de Pizan wrote.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Allegorical dialogue was a standard medieval vehicle for intellectual argument.

stimulus:
Around 1400, a war of words raged among French writers over the nature of women. Male authors cited the popular 'Romance of the Rose' to argue that women were deceitful and inferior; Christine de Pizan answered with the 'Book of the City of Ladies,' defending women's moral and intellectual worth. This literary quarrel drew in many writers on both sides.

The quarrel had been ignited by the 'Romance of the Rose,' the most widely read poem of the age, whose second author, Jean de Meun, portrayed women as vain, lustful, and deceitful. De Pizan's public letters attacking the poem — the first literary quarrel in French in which a woman took part — drew replies from the leading intellectuals of Paris, including the royal secretary Jean de Montreuil. Her 'City of Ladies' (1405) was her fullest answer: an entire imagined city built from the examples of accomplished women, offered as refutation. The quarrel over women — the querelle des femmes — would run for another two centuries, but de Pizan's intervention remains its most famous opening salvo: the first time a woman answered the learned misogyny of the schools in print, on its own terms.
stem: De Pizan's work belongs to which late-medieval intellectual controversy?
options: (A) The controversy over the sale of indulgences
(B) The dispute about the legitimacy of charging interest on loans
(C) The querelle des femmes, the literary debate over women's nature and worth
(D) The debate over whether the pope or church councils held supreme authority
explanation: De Pizan was the most prominent voice on one side of the querelle des femmes — the centuries-long literary debate about women's character and capacities. Her 'City of Ladies' was a direct rebuttal to misogynist literature, which places her work squarely in that controversy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The indulgence controversy became central later, with the Reformation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The usury debate concerned economics and church law, not the status of women.
option_explanations.C: Correct. De Pizan's defense of women was a landmark contribution to the querelle des femmes.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. That is the conciliarism debate, about church governance, not gender.

stimulus: A diagram shows a mountainside cut into a staircase of flat, stone-walled platforms. Each level holds soil for planting, with channels directing water from one terrace to the next. The caption identifies the system as Andean terrace agriculture.
stem: Unlike the chinampa system of the Valley of Mexico, which managed water on a lake bed, the technique shown here was developed primarily to address which environmental challenge?
options: (A) Steep mountain slopes with little flat land for planting
(B) Seasonal flooding of broad river plains
(C) Salty soils near coastal lagoons
(D) Dense jungle that had to be cleared by slash-and-burn
explanation: Terraces solve the problem of slope: they carve flat planting surfaces out of mountainsides, slow runoff, and control erosion. The two great intensive systems of the pre-Columbian Americas were answers to opposite environments — chinampas to watery lake beds, terraces to steep Andean slopes.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Terracing creates farmable flat land where the terrain offers almost none.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Floodplain farming needs drainage or flood control, not staircases cut into hillsides.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Salinity is a wetland and irrigation problem, addressed by systems like chinampas, not terraces.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Jungle clearance was handled by swidden (slash-and-burn) agriculture, not stone terracing.

stimulus: Before 1450, farmers in Afro-Eurasia plowed with oxen, horses, and water buffalo, while farmers in the Americas worked their fields without any comparable draft animals. The largest domesticated animals in the Andes — llamas and alpacas — were used as pack animals, not for pulling plows.
stem: Compared with Afro-Eurasian farming, a distinctive feature of pre-1450 American agriculture was that it developed with
options: (A) no fertilizer of any kind
(B) almost no large draft animals to pull plows
(C) no use of irrigation in any form whatsoever
(D) no domesticated plants at all
explanation: The Americas lacked the suite of large draft animals — horses, oxen, water buffalo — that powered Afro-Eurasian plow agriculture. American farmers compensated with intensive techniques like terracing, chinampas, and raised beds, worked by human labor. This is one of the sharpest contrasts between the two hemispheres' agricultural histories.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. American farmers used fertilizers such as guano and ash.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The absence of draft animals shaped American farming toward labor-intensive methods.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Irrigation was widespread in the Americas, from Andean canals to Mesoamerican systems.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Americas domesticated maize, potatoes, beans, squash, and many other crops.

stimulus: A diagram shows a mountainside cut into a staircase of flat, stone-walled platforms for planting — Andean terrace agriculture. Under the Inca, such projects were built by the mit'a, a labor system in which communities owed the state rotating drafts of workers for public works.
stem: After the Spanish conquest, the labor system associated with the technique shown was
options: (A) converted into a voluntary wage-labor market
(B) adapted by colonial authorities into forced labor drafts for the silver mines at Potosí
(C) abolished entirely as incompatible with Spanish law
(D) replaced immediately by enslaved African labor in the highlands
explanation: The Spanish kept the Inca institution and redirected it: the colonial mita drafted Andean communities to work the silver mines of Potosí under brutal conditions. It is a clear case of colonizers adapting an Indigenous institution to extract wealth, not inventing a new system from scratch.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The mita was coerced rotational labor, not a free market in wages.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The colonial mita funneled Andean labor into Potosí's silver mines.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Spanish preserved the mit'a because it was useful; they did not abolish it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Enslaved African labor was concentrated on coastal plantations, not highland mining, where the mita supplied workers.
